name: Greenlandic Inuktitut
confidence_why: Bergsland 1955, Fortescue 1984, Nagano-Madsen 1993 and the acoustic study of Jacobsen 2000 all find that West Greenlandic has no phonemic or demarcative word stress, the prominence heard on the last or antepenultimate vowel being the phrase-final pitch contour, so the fixed final-stress coding taken from Gordon 2002's survey table has no first-hand support.
catalog_quote: Stress does not play any contrastive or demarcative role in West Greenlandic. There may however be an auditory impression of relative stress on heavy syllables in connection with the intonational nucleus that covers the last morae of word forms, as discussed below (i.e. when the pitch peak of the nucleus coincides with a heavy syllable). See Rischel 1974, p. 91ff, for fluctuating judgments in the…
sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title, Jacobsen 2000 (Phonetica 57: 40-67), is squarely about word stress in West Greenlandic and contradicts the catalog's fixed-dominant final coding: its abstract concludes 'Greenlandic prosody does not include an autonomous stress category'. Full text remains closed on every access channel checked (OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, OpenAIRE; the DOI now lands at degruyterbrill.com, Karger could not be reached by automated download); only the PubMed abstract is. Priority high for acquisition (online with a university library login). Re-read on-disk material corroborates: Nagano-Madsen 1993:147 (no lexical stress or accent; perceived prominence = H of the terminal contour) and Arnhold, Elfner & Compton 2023 ms pp. 5-7 (Rischel 1974:91 'no well-defined status', listeners split between antepenultimate and final vowel = the two H points of the word-final HLH contour; Jacobsen finds no autonomous stress). Recommendation unchanged from the earlier reading: reclassify kala1399 to no-word-stress (domain word) with Fortescue 1984:339 as the full-text deciding quote and Jacobsen 2000 abstract + Nagano-Madsen 1993:147 as backing; note the word-final HLH contour as the source of Gordon 2002's 'final'.

new_statements.reading: The only instrumental study devoted to West Greenlandic stress finds no autonomous word-stress category: what listeners hear as prominence is the word-final HLH pitch contour on the last vowel morae (high on the antepenultimate and final mora) plus syllable-weight duration, not stress. This flatly contradicts the catalog's fixed-dominant 'final' coding, which rests only on Gordon 2002's appendix line with no quotation. It agrees with the catalog's own domain quote (Fortescue 1984:339, 'Stress does not play any contrastive or demarcative role in West Greenlandic') and with Nagano-Madsen 1993:147 (held by the project, read this search of works with stress in the title: 'there is no lexical category of stress or accent in West Greenlandic Eskimo. The perceived prominence was found to coincide with the high tone of the terminal contour'). Caveat: abstract only; the full paper (pp. 40-67) is paywalled at De Gruyter Brill.

sources.quote: The main purpose is to investigate whether stress is a relevant category in Greenlandic word prosody. I focus on tonal and durational parameters. The data material consists of word lists read aloud seven times by two subjects. The main findings are: (1) The prosodic characteristics of words can be explained in either tonal or durational terms. [...] It is concluded that Greenlandic prosody does not include an autonomous stress category, either tonal or durational parameters alone will do.
sources.note: Dedicated acoustic study of West Greenlandic word prosody (word lists, two speakers, seven repetitions, f0 and duration). Conclusion: no autonomous stress category in Greenlandic prosody; the word-level prominence pattern is reducible to tone (the word-final HLH contour on the last vowel morae) or to duration (syllable weight: short/long/overlong). No stress-placement rule is given because stress is denied. sources.citation: Nagano-Madsen, Yasuko. 1993. Phrase-final intonation in West Greenlandic Eskimo. Working Papers (Lund University, Dept. of Linguistics) 40: 145-155.
sources.quote: p.146: "What is now recognized as being an element of phrase-final intonation manifestation on the last three vowel morae (Rischel 1974) has earlier been interpreted as 'musical accent' (Thalbitzer 1904) or 'stress' (Pyle 1970). Both Rischel and Nagano-Madsen 1992 treat the language as having no lexical stress or accent and as being mora-counting." p.147: "As already mentioned, there is no lexical category of stress or accent in West Greenlandic Eskimo. The perceived prominence was found to coincide with the high tone of the terminal contour, be that phrase-internal or phrase-final."

sources.quote: p.1 (Abstract): "The main analysis is based on original data from South Baffin Island Inuktitut (Uqqurmiut), but the chapter also examines the literature on other varieties from across the language family." p.5: "The notion of stress or accent had been used in early descriptions of Inuit (e.g. Pyle 1970, p. 131), but Rischel (1974, p. 91) concludes that it has no well-defined status in West Greenlandic. He further states that it is difficult to obtain agreement on stress placement, although both native speakers and phonetically trained Danish listeners tend to hear stress on either the antepenultimate or the last vowel." p.7: "Jacobsen (2000) therefore concludes that there is no autonomous category of stress in West Greenlandic phonology." p.34: "duration, f0 and intensity did not consistently point towards a specific syllable as most prominent in the present data, similar to Jacobsen’s (2000) findings for West Greenlandic."
